summary: Offers suggestions on how IEEE 802.1X authenticators should use RADIUS. The material also appears as a non-normative appendix in the IEEE 802.1X specification and is published as an RFC for information. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Wi-Fi and network ports can ask a central server who may join. This memo gives tips for how those ports should talk to that server.

questions: how to assign vlan with radius tunnel attributes
what is the rc4 eapol-key frame
subtitle: How a switch or Wi-Fi access point should fill in RADIUS messages when it checks who may join the network.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.1X lets a network port demand authentication, and many ports use a central RADIUS server for it. RADIUS was designed for dial-up, so it was unclear how its attributes apply to Ethernet and 802.11 ports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC goes through the RADIUS accounting and authentication attributes one by one and says how an 802.1X Authenticator should use, fill in or ignore each. It also describes the RC4 EAPOL-Key frame used to hand out keys.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC whose material also sits in a non-normative appendix of IEEE 802.1X. It is updated by RFC 7268, and its own text warns that the EAPOL-Key frame was likely to be deprecated.

today: RFC 3580 is Informational and is updated by RFC 7268. Its own text expects the RC4 EAPOL-Key frame it describes to be deprecated once the IEEE 802.11 enhanced security work is complete.

sections.title: Why 802.1X Needs RADIUS Guidelines
sections.content:
IEEE 802.1X provides network port authentication for IEEE 802 media, including Ethernet, Token Ring and 802.11 wireless LANs. It does not require a backend Authentication Server, so it can run on a stand-alone bridge or Access Point. When an operator wants central authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA), the Authenticator is expected to act as a RADIUS client.

RADIUS support is optional in IEEE 802.1X, which is why this document is Informational and why its material is also included in a non-normative appendix of the IEEE 802.1X specification. The roles are: the Supplicant is the device being authenticated, the Authenticator is the bridge or Access Point that demands authentication, and the Authentication Server checks the credentials.
sections.eli5: A building has a guard at the door (the port) and a security office (the server). Not every building has an office, but if yours does, this memo says how the guard should talk to it.

sections.title: Accounting Attributes
sections.content:
With a few exceptions, the RADIUS accounting attributes from RFC 2866, RFC 2867 and RFC 2869 mean the same thing in 802.1X sessions as in dial-up sessions. The RFC discusses three that need extra care.

Acct-Terminate-Cause says why a session ended. The RFC maps each 802.1X termination cause to a RADIUS value, for example a Supplicant logoff becomes User Request (1) and a lost physical connection becomes Lost Carrier (2). Successful re-authentication does not end a session, so no accounting packet is sent unless the session status changes. If authorizations change after re-authentication, the Service Unavailable (15) cause is used and the rest of the session is accounted as a separate session.

Acct-Multi-Session-Id links the related sessions of a Supplicant that roams between Access Points. The suggested form concatenates the original AP MAC address, the Supplicant MAC address and a 64-bit NTP timestamp, written as an ASCII string of hex digits. Acct-Link-Count may be used to account for the number of aggregated ports.
sections.eli5: When a visitor leaves, the guard writes down why: they asked to leave, they walked out of range, or the guard sent them away. If a visitor moves between guards, a special ticket number lets the office see it was one visit.

sections.title: Authentication Attributes
sections.content:
Section 3 walks through the attributes of RADIUS authentication. Many do not apply to 802.1X: User-Password, CHAP-Password and CHAP-Challenge are not used because 802.1X does not support PAP or CHAP, Framed-Protocol has no value for IEEE 802 media, and attributes such as Callback-Number are not understood by 802.1X Authenticators.

Several are filled in in a specific way. NAS-IP-Address holds the IPv4 address of the bridge or Access Point, and a loopback address is suggested when there are several interfaces. NAS-Port holds the bridge port number, or for an Access Point the 16-bit association ID. Called-Station-Id holds the bridge or AP MAC address as upper-case ASCII with octets separated by hyphens, and the SSID SHOULD be appended after a colon when it is known. Calling-Station-Id holds the Supplicant MAC address in the same format. Service-Type is most commonly Framed (2), Authenticate Only (8) or Call Check (10).

Framed-MTU is set by the Authenticator to the value for the medium, and the server may send an EAP packet as large as Framed-MTU minus four octets. For Ethernet that value is 1500 and for 802.11 it is 2304, but because some 802.11 stations cannot handle more than 1500 octets, servers are advised to send EAP packets no larger than 1496 octets when the NAS-Port-Type is 802.11.

Session-Timeout has several meanings. With Termination-Action RADIUS-Request it sets the time before re-authentication, and in an Access-Challenge it tells the Authenticator how long to wait for an EAP-Response. The Message-Authenticator attribute MUST be used to protect packets within a RADIUS/EAP conversation, and EAP packets travel in the EAP-Message attribute defined in RFC 3579.
sections.eli5: The guard has a long form to fill in. Some boxes do not apply to a door guard and are left empty. Others are filled in a set way, such as writing the visitor's device address in capital letters with dashes between the pairs.

sections.title: VLAN Assignment and the RC4 EAPOL-Key Frame
sections.content:
The RFC explains how RADIUS tunnel attributes can place a port into a particular Virtual LAN (VLAN) based on the authentication result. The attributes are Tunnel-Type=VLAN (13), Tunnel-Medium-Type=802 and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID=VLANID. The VLAN ID is 12 bits with a value between 1 and 4094 inclusive, and it is encoded as a string. The RFC gives the example of letting a wireless host stay on the same VLAN as it moves around a campus network. If only the VLAN ID is wanted, the Tag field SHOULD be set to zero in all tunnel attributes.

Section 4 describes the RC4 EAPOL-Key frame, which the Authenticator sends to give the Supplicant keying material, for example the 802.11 "default" key shared by all Stations in a broadcast domain or a unicast "key mapping" key. The frame is not acknowledged, so if it is lost the two sides do not share keys and communication fails; the usual remedy is to run authentication again. The key can either be carried encrypted in the frame, or be absent, in which case the Key Length least significant octets of the MS-MPPE-Send-Key attribute are used as keying material.
sections.eli5: After the check, the office can tell the guard which room the visitor belongs in (the VLAN). The guard can also hand over a secret code for the visitor's messages, but the guard never learns whether the visitor got the note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using RADIUS for 802.1X inherits all the threats present in other RADIUS applications. The RFC lists packet modification or forgery, dictionary attacks, known plaintext attacks, replay, outcome mismatches, 802.11 integration and key management issues.

Because 802.1X is based on EAP, the Message-Authenticator attribute MUST protect all Access-Request, Access-Challenge, Access-Accept and Access-Reject packets that carry an EAP-Message, so all RADIUS packets used with 802.1X MUST be authenticated and integrity protected. Implementations SHOULD support IPsec with IKE, and the RADIUS shared secret is preferably at least 16 octets. The same shared secret MUST NOT be used for both 802.1X authentication and PAP authentication. To avoid outcome mismatches, such as an EAP Success inside an Access-Reject, the Authenticator makes its decision solely on Access-Accept or Access-Reject, not on the EAP-Message contents.

The RFC is frank about the EAPOL-Key frame. It is likely to be deprecated when the IEEE 802.11 enhanced security work completes, and it has known weaknesses: some implementations use only default keys, the same keying material (MS-MPPE-Recv-Key) is reused for more than one purpose, and the RC4 key encryption has weaknesses similar to WEP. Implementors are urged to consult the 802.11 enhanced security specification for a more secure alternative.
sections.eli5: The phone line between guard and office has to be protected from people who listen in or fake a call. The old secret-code trick the guard uses is weak, so the memo says to use something better when it exists.

viz.caption: 802.1X TERMINATION CAUSES AND THEIR RADIUS VALUES (RFC 3580)

items.label: User Request
items.desc: 802.1X SupplicantLogoff(1): the session ended because of an EAPOL-Logoff from the Supplicant.

items.label: Lost Carrier
items.desc: 802.1X portFailure(2): physical connectivity was lost for reasons other than roaming.

items.label: Supplicant Restart
items.desc: 802.1X SupplicantRestart(3): the Supplicant state machines were re-initialized.

items.label: Admin Reset
items.desc: 802.1X authControlForceUnauth(5): the port was forced into the unauthorized state.

items.label: Port Reinitialized
items.desc: 802.1X portReInit(6): the port's MAC was reinitialized.

items.label: Port Administratively Disabled
items.desc: 802.1X portAdminDisabled(7): the port was administratively disabled.

items.title: Tunnel-Private-Group-ID
items.text: Carries the VLAN ID as a string; the ID is 12 bits, from 1 to 4094.

items.title: Tag field
items.text: Set to zero when only the VLAN ID is specified.
